newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish poet happy but nervous over Nobel prize.
newsitem.headline: Polish poet happy but nervous over Nobel prize.

text.p: Polish poet Wislawa Szymborska, shy 73-year-old winner of this year's Nobel Literature Prize, said on Thursday she was very pleased but also apprehensive at the prospect of intense worldwide attention.

"This is a difficult situation. I am normally a very private person and now I forsee some difficult moments," Szymborska, laughing with excitement, said by telephone from a hotel for writers in the mountain resort of Zakopane.
"I am very pleased for Polish literature although there are other poets like me in Poland...Tadeusz Rozewicz and Zbigniew Herbert to mention only two," Szymborska told Reuters.
She said that, although she had been named among the candidates, her award from the Swedish academy -- which is worth $1.12 million -- had come as a surprise.
Szymborska paid warm tribute to Anders Bodegard, Swedish translator of her poems, which the academy recognised were hard to put into other languages due to their stylistic variety.
"If this had been a mediocre translator we would not be talking today," she said. She herself translates French poetry.
Asked whether she would now appear more in public and perhaps lecture abroad, the slight, grey-haired poet said she did not yet know, but commented: "No, I never give lectures."

Ex-president Lech Walesa said he was possibly more excited to hear of Szymborska's award than he had been to learn of his own 1983 Nobel Peace prize, awarded when he was interned by communist authorities as leader of the Solidarity labour union.
"A woman has been recognised, who is so modest as a person and so great of heart and pen," Walesa told reporters at his office in Solidarity headquarters in the Baltic city of Gdansk.
Current President Aleksander Kwasniewski wrote to her that the achievement was above all her own, but thanked her for contributing greatly to the fame of Poles and Poland.
Earlier this week Szymborska won the Polish PEN Club's poetry award and Polish literary critics were overjoyed at the Nobel literature award, the fifth to go to a Pole or Polish-born writer.

"We could not believe it at first. She was a candidate we put forward many times," Jacek Bochenski, the Pen Club's deputy president, told Reuters. "Her poetry is profound, beautiful, full of humour, simple," he said.
Stanislaw Lem, who like Szymborska lives in the city of Krakow, said: "Wiska (Wislawa) simply deserved this prize."
The high-brow science fiction author pointed out that poet Czeslaw Milosz had won the 1980 literature prize, adding that this showed Poland's poetry was greater than its prose.
Milosz, who lives in the United States, told RMF-FM radio he was glad, as he was a great admirer of Szymborska's work.
"Above all, this is a great triumph of Polish 20th century poetry," he said.
Earlier Polish winners are novelists Henryk Sienkiewicz in 1905 and Wladyslaw Reymont in 1924. Polish-born Jewish novelist Isaac Bashevis Singer, who wrote in Yiddish, won the 1978 prize.
Critic Jan Pieszczachowicz, who has written extensively on Szymborska, commented that her poetry avoided the slightly hysterical tone of much 20th century literature.
"Szymborska, with an unchanging stoical smile, informs her readers that things are not so bad," he told PAP news agency.
The award to Szymborska surprised observers who had expected a novelist to win after Irish poet Seamus Heaney, who was due to visit Krakow on Thursday, took last year's prize.

Szymborska, also a literary critic, has published several slim volumes of poetry since Stalinist censorship was lifted in 1957 -- she has disowned earlier poems which reflected Stalinist-era literary style and content.
Her poetry includes "Calling out to the Yeti" (1957), "People on the Bridge" (1986) and "The End and the Beginning" written in 1993.
